value.overview: Leach’s Storm-Petrel is a small, long-winged seabird that spends most of its life over deep ocean waters. It breeds colonially on remote islands in northern oceans and disperses widely across tropical and subtropical seas outside the breeding season. The species has a distinctive bounding, bat-like flight and often picks small prey from the sea surface while hovering. It is rarely seen from shore because it usually remains far offshore.
value.classification: Leach’s Storm-Petrel belongs to the order Procellariiformes and family Hydrobatidae, the northern storm-petrels. Its scientific name is Hydrobates leucorhous.
value.identification: This medium-sized storm-petrel has dark brown to nearly black upperparts, long pointed wings, a deeply notched tail, and a pale diagonal bar across each upperwing. Many birds show a white rump divided by a narrow dark line, although rump color varies among populations and some Pacific birds are dark-rumped. It has a bouncy, erratic flight with frequent twists and turns. Identification at sea can be difficult because plumage varies and several storm-petrels have similar shapes.
value.rangeHabitat: Leach’s Storm-Petrel breeds on remote coastal islands in the North Atlantic and North Pacific, nesting in burrows, rock crevices, or dense vegetation. Outside the breeding season it disperses over tropical and subtropical ocean waters, generally far from land and over areas with productive surface waters. In Costa Rica it is a pelagic, nonbreeding visitor recorded in offshore waters, particularly during ocean voyages and seabird surveys; it is not known to breed in the country. Sightings from land are unusual.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant and oceanic disperser. Birds breeding in northern Atlantic and Pacific colonies move south after breeding into tropical waters. In Costa Rica, it occurs as an uncommon offshore visitor rather than a resident or breeding species.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in colonies on isolated islands, often where predators are absent or limited. Pairs nest in burrows, under rocks, or among vegetation and usually lay a single egg. Adults return to colonies mainly at night, which reduces exposure to predators. Incubation and chick-rearing are extended compared with many small birds, and young birds remain dependent on stored energy and food brought by both parents. Colonies may contain thousands or millions of birds, depending on the site.
value.dietFeeding: The diet includes small fish, squid, crustaceans, plankton, and other small marine organisms. Leach’s Storm-Petrels commonly feed by hovering or pattering over the water and picking prey from the surface, although they may also take food associated with plankton patches, floating material, or predatory fish. They may forage alone or join mixed flocks of storm-petrels and other seabirds where prey is concentrated.
value.behavior: This species is strongly oceanic and spends nearly all of its nonbreeding life at sea. Its flight is distinctive but somewhat erratic, combining shallow wingbeats, glides, and sudden changes of direction close to the water. It is generally solitary or found in small groups, although larger feeding concentrations can form. Adults visit breeding colonies mainly after dark, and the species has a highly developed sense of smell that may help it locate food and nesting colonies.

conservation.populationTrend: Decreasing. Declines have been documented or inferred in multiple breeding populations, although the strength of available monitoring varies among regions.
conservation.threats: Important threats include introduced rats and other predators at breeding colonies, disturbance and habitat degradation on nesting islands, artificial lighting that attracts fledglings, fisheries bycatch, marine pollution, and changes in ocean conditions that affect prey availability. Climate change may increase pressure on colonies and alter feeding conditions. Because Costa Rica supports the species only in offshore waters, national conservation attention is most relevant to marine pollution, sustainable fisheries, and protection of pelagic seabirds.
conservation.howToHelp: Protecting predator-free breeding islands, removing invasive mammals from colonies, reducing artificial light near seabird nesting and fledging areas, and improving monitoring are key measures. At sea, reducing accidental capture through effective seabird bycatch controls, preventing plastic and oil pollution, and supporting sustainable fisheries can help. In Costa Rica, reporting offshore sightings through established bird-monitoring programs and supporting marine protected areas and responsible fishing practices can improve knowledge and conservation.
